Hello,

I have question to all of you who are familiar with MIT's idea of displaying holograms using AOM. 

One idea of computing holograms is to use bipolar intensity. 

OK, it sounds really easy to calculate those fringes... I guess it's also easy to display that fringes on any real-amplitude-modulating matrix (or just print it out on some transparencies), It's also easy to represent that fringes in GrayScale

But I got really confused... AOM modulates PHASE only! 

How do they convert computed amplitude-grating structure into phase-grating structure?

One thing more.. if AOM can be phase hologram, why not to compute phase hologram, without need of using reference beam?

Do you have any ideas?

Thanks

Maciej

posts.content_md:
Hi - 

Are you referring to the older Mark I and Mark II MIT spatial imaging group systems?

I am under the impression that the AOM acts as an acoustically-modulated "grating." Or hologram, really, as it carries multiple superimposed waves. The light is de-scanned by a counter-rotating scanner. (Is this what you are asking?) I am not sure that I understand your question about phase- versus amplitude-modulation.

Several of their detailed publications and Ph.D. theses are available at [their site](http://www.media.mit.edu/spi/spiPubs.htm), which you are probably already familiar with.

Gregg

Dear Gregg, 

Thank you for answer, and Im sorry my question wasn't clear. 

Let me try to make it more clear;

- Yes, reffering to Mark I. I'm not asking about scanners, or construction of display. I'm asking what informations are actually transfered to AOM.

- AOM acts as (is) acustically modulated grating. It is PHASE grating (phase modulating grating) - which means it's modulating phase of beam, and it is not modulating real amplidude of that beam. 

The result of bipolar intensity computation method is the pattern of darker-and-brighter fringes. So it was calculated to be displayed on any amplitude modulating grating (as a darker fringes on transparent film). All phase information was coded using reference beam. That kind of coding is necessary if we are using real-amplitude modulating matrix (i.e. holographic film that can record intensity only) 

But my question is: 

Why to code phase information, when AOM is modulating phase only ? Why AOM is not acting as kinoform?

AOM is actually acting as pure-phase-hologram, so why do they calculate fringes like for pure-amplitude-hologram.

Why do compute intensity instead of phase shifting. 

hmm... i hope you feel what my problem is....

waiting for your answer

regards

Maciej

posts.author: favalora
posts.content_md:
Sorry, I hit "submit" too soon.

Regarding your question about the algorithms used to generate the imagery, I think there is a simple way of understanding it which I might ironically be unable to express clearly here this evening.

Basically, their algorithms compute what the 3-D scene looks like from a variety of viewpoints, and then modulate a bunch of "basis fringes" (varying frequency carriers) with the amplitudes that are intended to be seen from those viewpoints. These are summed together, launched down the AOM, and then de-scanned to counteract the fact that the time-varying holographic data are flying down the AOM.

If you're familiar with electronic 3-D displays, it's conceptually similar to multi-view displays. Dr. Lucente refers to this as "diffraction-specific" computation. In my opinion, it's a good method because you can quickly compute what a scene looks like from many points of view, and then "weight" the basis vectors with those data. This is faster than using brute-force to compute the contributions of each point in the image, etc. etc. It ends up in basically the same information (although I suppose the phase might be ignored.)

If this is unclear, it's my fault. You can probably find a better explanation in Chapter 4 of his thesis [(PDF)](http://www.lucente.us/pubs/PhDthesis/4.pdf).

-g

AOM is always phase modulating. The result of modulation may be different;

**a)** kinoform-like phase modulation *(where shape of hologram is simmilar to image wavefront (no interference pattern is recorded)- thats why we can not really talk about diffraction. only 1 image is produced*

**b)** "normal" optical-phase-hologram-like modulation Interference pattern is recorded as a phase grating which (I believe) works same way as amplitude grating.

I thought (and thats why i was confused) AOM in holography can work in the "a" mode (kinoform-like). It's easy (i believe) to compute shape of the wavefront, and transfer it to phase changes in AOM. **But it's not working this way** 

AOM works in "b" mode-- that's why it's OK to compute interference pattern, and record that pattern in phase modulating medium (just like oprical recording of hologram).

OK, now It's kinda clear for me...

BUT still few more questions left

**1)** Why they didn't compute holograms in holovideo in "a" way? it seems to be easier for me (faster) and it produces 1 imgage only

**2)** if they computed holograms using reference beam (*and they they did -> interference based computation*) why there is only single image reconstructed (where is conjucted image?). Please note that interference-based-computation is used also for LCD displays. 

> Dr. Lucente refers to this as "diffraction-specific" computation.
 Yes... I do know it... But they are somtimes using interference based computation for Mark displays as well.

posts.author: favalora
posts.content_md:
Hi - 

Regarding your first set of questions, I unfortunately don't know the answer to that. I am not familiar enough with the physics of AOMs. I like to think about it "one level up," which is as an agile beam-steering device with non-zero length and the ability to launch beams in multiple directions at once from each small region of the AOM.

You suggest its inability to elicit accommodation responses. I don't think that the MIT group ever measured that. Howver, I believe that it is theoretically quite capable of generating good reconstructions of light fields, even if they are horizontal-parallax only, and even if Mark I and Mark II had some scan-line clarity issues. For example, some researchers in Japan believe that you can cause accomodation if you have a sufficient number of "views" - the researcher called it the "super multiview condition." Perhaps the MIT system is capable of that too.

I don't know how the eye focuses in response to highly astigmatic imagery, such as HPO holograms.

Actually, I would like to know more about what cues cause the eye to focus. I have spoken with several vision experts but am not satisfied with the answers I hear yet; perhaps that is still an area of advanced research. I wonder if one problem is that researchers can't create good experimental stimulii yet! That is, I wonder if they need a good full-parallax display in order to do the experiments they need.

You asked about my opinions on the viability of electro-holographic versus multi-view displays that, for example, use multiple projectors or time-multiplexed view scanning. I think that both are promising. In my opinion, non-holographic displays have the advantage today, because in 2007 it is easier to reconstruct 3-D light fields with multiple fast projectors than to create arbitrary diffraction patterns. However, I would guess that this will change. I have a feeling that holography could win, but I don't know how many years it will take for this to occur. 2 years? 10?

For example, [we](http://www.actuality-systems.com) built a display in 2003 or 2004 that generated an image from a flat panel with - believe it or not - 198 views across about 30 degrees. It was 4" big and 4" deep. It was *very* believable; it was the only flat-panel multiview display whose imagery I involuntarily reached out to grab. (How did it work? Here's [one description.](http://appft1.uspto.gov/netacgi/nph-Parser?Sect1=PTO1&Sect2=HITOFF&d=PG01&p=1&u=%2Fnetahtml%2FPTO%2Fsrchnum.html&r=1&f=G&l=50&s1=%2220050270645%22.PGNR.&OS=DN/20050270645&RS=DN/20050270645))

-Gregg
